title: Acoustic impedance and reflection
goals: Work out a material's acoustic impedance from its density and velocity
Work out how much of the sound reflects and how much crosses a boundary
Explain why a back wall or an air-filled crack echoes so strongly, and why a probe needs couplant
Tell when an echo comes back upside down
summary:
**Acoustic impedance** is how hard a material is to set moving by sound: $Z = \rho v$, density (kg/m³) times velocity (m/s), in rayl. The numbers are big, so they are quoted in **MRayl** (millions). Typical values: air 0.0004, water 1.5, perspex 3.2, aluminium 17, steel 46.5 MRayl.

**At a boundary** met square on, the share of the intensity (energy) that comes back is

$$R = \left(\frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2$$

and the rest goes on: $T = 1 - R$. Difference over sum, squared. The bigger the mismatch, the more comes back.

- **Water to steel:** about 88% back, 12% in. That is why the front-wall echo is so big in immersion testing.
- **Steel to air:** more than 99.99% back. That is why back walls and air-filled cracks echo so well, and why a probe needs **couplant**.
- **Equal impedances:** nothing reflects, whatever the materials.

**The amplitude ratio** $r = \frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}$ compares the height of the echo with the wave coming in; $R = r^2$. $r$ is minus when the sound meets a lower impedance: the echo comes back **upside down**. The square removes the sign, so $R$ is the same either way.

**The method:** $r$ first, square it for $R$, then $T = 1 - R$.

**Decibels:** energies (like $T$) use $10\log_{10}$; echo heights use $20\log_{10}$.

Impedance decides how **much** comes back; velocity and time decide **when** ($d = \frac{vt}{2}$).

cards.q: Ultrasound travelling through water meets a flat steel surface square on. Roughly how much of its energy goes into the steel?
options: None: water cannot pass sound into steel
cards.why: Only about 12% gets in; about 88% reflects. Water and steel resist sound very differently (their **acoustic impedances**, about 1.5 and 46.5 MRayl, are far apart), and a big mismatch sends most of the sound back. It is not none: immersion testing works on that 12%.

cards.title: Acoustic impedance
cards.body:
Every material resists being set moving by sound. That resistance is its **acoustic impedance**:

$$Z = \rho v$$

$Z$ is the impedance, $\rho$ (rho) the material's **density** in kg/m³, and $v$ the speed of sound in it, in m/s. Multiply them. The unit is kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, called the **rayl**. The numbers are big, so they are usually given in **MRayl** (millions of rayl): steel is about 46.5 MRayl.

Where two materials meet, what matters is how different their impedances are. A small difference lets most of the sound through; a big one sends most of it back.
cards.more:
Think of pushing a child's swing and then pushing a car. The light thing is easy to set moving; the heavy one resists. Impedance is that resistance for sound. Dense materials that carry sound fast (steel) have a high impedance; light ones that carry it slowly (air) have a tiny one.

Numbers: water, density 1000 kg/m³, sound at 1480 m/s: $Z = 1000 \times 1480 = 1\,480\,000$ rayl, which is 1.48 MRayl. Aluminium: $2700 \times 6320 = 17\,064\,000$ rayl, about 17.1 MRayl. Steel's is nearly three times aluminium's, even though sound is slower in steel, because steel is nearly three times as dense.

To get MRayl, divide by 1 000 000.

cards.q: Steel: density {rho} kg/m³, longitudinal velocity {v} m/s. What is its acoustic impedance?
cards.hint: Density times velocity, then divide by 1 000 000 for MRayl.

cards.title: What comes back
cards.body:
Where sound meets a boundary square on, some goes on and some comes back. Call the material it comes from 1 and the one it meets 2. The share of the sound's **intensity** (its energy) that comes back is

$$R = \left(\frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2$$

Take the difference, divide by the sum, square it. $R$ is a fraction: 0.88 means 88%. The rest goes on: $T = 1 - R$.

Water (1.48) to steel (46.5): $\frac{45.02}{47.98} = 0.94$, squared 0.88. So 88% comes back and 12% goes in. Try other pairs.
cards.more:
In words: the more different the two impedances, the nearer the fraction gets to 1, and the more comes back.

Perspex (3.22) to steel (46.5): $\frac{43.28}{49.72} = 0.87$, squared 0.76: 76% back. Aluminium (17.1) to steel (46.5): $\frac{29.4}{63.6} = 0.46$, squared 0.21: only 21% back, because the two metals are closer.

Why squared? The fraction in the brackets compares the heights of the waves (their amplitudes). Energy goes with the height squared, as the power in a resistor goes with the voltage squared.

And $T = 1 - R$ because no energy is lost at the boundary itself: what does not come back goes on.

cards.q: Water ($Z_1$ = {z1} MRayl) meets steel ($Z_2$ = {z2} MRayl). What percentage of the intensity is reflected?
cards.why: Close to 88%. That is why in immersion testing the front-wall echo is so large, and only about an eighth of the sound gets into the steel.
cards.hint: Difference over sum, then square. Times 100 for a percentage.

cards.title: Big mismatch, big echo
cards.body:
The further apart $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are, the more comes back.

- **Steel to air** (46.5 against 0.0004 MRayl): more than 99.99% reflected. That is why the back wall of a plate echoes so well, and why a crack, full of air, shows up.
- **Probe to part through an air gap**: almost nothing gets in. So you fill the gap with **couplant**: gel, oil or water.
- **Equal impedances**: $Z_2 - Z_1 = 0$, so nothing reflects, however different the two materials are.
cards.more:
Tie a rope to a second rope just like it and a flick runs straight through: nothing comes back. Tie it to a wall, a huge mismatch, and the flick comes all the way back. Sound at a boundary behaves the same.

Steel to air in numbers: $\frac{0.0004 - 46.5}{0.0004 + 46.5} = -0.99998$; squared, 0.99997. So 99.997% reflected, 0.003% through. Even a film of air far thinner than a millimetre does this, which is why a dry probe shows nothing but its own pulse.

With water in the gap, water to steel lets in about 12%: not much, but enough to test with. Gels, a little closer to steel, do slightly better.

cards.intro: Set the first material to **steel** and the second to **air**: a probe with nothing between it and the part, or the far side of a plate.

ask.q: What happens at a steel to air boundary?
options: Almost all the sound is reflected
Almost all of it goes into the air
None is reflected, because air has no impedance
ask.why: Air's impedance is around 0.0004 MRayl against steel's 46, so $R$ is 99.99%. That is why the back wall reflects so well, and why a probe needs couplant.

cards.title: Upside-down echoes
cards.body:
$R$ is about energy. The height of the reflected wave itself, compared with the wave coming in, is the **amplitude ratio**, small $r$, with no square:

$$r = \frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}$$

and $R = r^2$.

$r$ is **negative** when the sound meets a **lower** impedance ($Z_2$ smaller than $Z_1$), as at steel to water or steel to air. A negative $r$ means the echo comes back **upside down** (its phase is flipped). Squaring removes the sign, so $R$ is the same whichever way the sound crosses.
cards.more:
Water (1.48) to steel (46.5): $r = \frac{46.5 - 1.48}{46.5 + 1.48} = \frac{45.02}{47.98} = 0.94$. Plus: the echo comes back the right way up, 94% as tall as the wave that went in.

Steel to water: $r = \frac{1.48 - 46.5}{47.98} = -0.94$. Just as tall, but upside down.

Squared, both give $R = 0.88$: 88% of the energy either way.

Most flaw detectors show a rectified A-scan (only the size of each echo), so you do not see the flip. On an RF display (the raw signal) you can: a back-wall echo from steel to air is upside down compared with an echo from a harder material.

cards.q: Is more intensity reflected going from water into steel, or from steel into water?
options: The same either way; only the phase of the reflection differs
cards.why: Swapping $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ only changes the sign inside the brackets, and the square removes it. The sign does matter for the wave itself: reflecting towards a lower impedance inverts it.
cards.hint: Swap $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ in the formula. What does squaring do to a minus sign?

cards.intro: The amplitude ratio $r = \frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}$ keeps its sign. Try steel to water, then water to steel.

ask.q: When $r$ is negative, what does that tell you?
options: The reflected wave is inverted: the sound met a lower impedance
ask.why: A negative $r$ means the reflection comes back upside down. On an RF display, a back-wall echo (steel to air) is inverted compared with an echo from a harder material.

cards.q: A perspex wedge ($Z$ = 3.22 MRayl) on steel ($Z$ = 46.5 MRayl). How much of the intensity crosses into the steel?
cards.why: Far better than water (about 12%) but still most of the sound comes back into the wedge, which is why wedges are shaped and damped to lose those reflections.

cards.q: Couplant gel ($Z$ = 2.42 MRayl) on steel ($Z$ = 46.5 MRayl). How much of the intensity crosses into the steel?
cards.why: The same three moves as the perspex wedge: $r$, then square it for $R$, then $T = 1 - R$. Gel lets in more than water (about 12%) because its impedance is a little closer to steel's.

cards.q: Same boundary: water {z1} MRayl, steel {z2} MRayl. What percentage of the intensity goes into the steel?
cards.why: What is not reflected is transmitted: $T = 1 - R$.

cards.q: Why is couplant needed between a contact probe and the part?
options: It replaces the air gap, whose impedance is so low that almost nothing would cross it
It lowers the part's velocity so echoes are easier to read
It stops the probe wearing out, and nothing else
cards.why: Even a thin layer of air reflects nearly everything, because air's impedance is tiny next to steel's. A liquid or gel has an impedance thousands of times closer, so sound can cross into the part. It does not change the part's velocity: the echoes are exactly where they would be.

cards.q: Aluminium: density {rho} kg/m³, velocity {v} m/s. Its impedance?
cards.why: About 17 MRayl: less than half of steel's, though aluminium's velocity is higher. Density matters as much as velocity.

cards.q: Two different materials happen to have the same acoustic impedance. What happens to sound crossing from one to the other?
options: It all goes through: nothing is reflected
It depends only on which has the higher density
cards.why: With $Z_1 = Z_2$ the top of the fraction is zero, so $R = 0$, however different their densities and velocities are.

cards.q: Match each material to its typical acoustic impedance.
cards.why: Typical values; they vary with the grade and temperature. Liquids and plastics sit in the low single figures, metals in the tens, air near nothing.

cards.q: In an immersion tank, why is the front-wall echo from a steel part so much bigger than the back-wall echo?
options: About 88% of the sound reflects at the water to steel surface, and what gets in loses more on the way back out
The probe is closer to the back wall
The back wall is always rough
cards.why: Most of the sound never enters. Of the 12% that does, the back-wall echo must cross the steel to water boundary again on the way out.

cards.q: At a boundary $Z_1$ = {z1} MRayl, $Z_2$ = {z2} MRayl. How much weaker in dB is the transmitted intensity than the incident?
cards.why: An intensity ratio in dB is $10\log_{10}$ (amplitudes use 20). Give it as a positive number of dB lost.
cards.hint: Work out $T$ as a fraction first. $T$ is an energy ratio, so use $10\log_{10}$ (echo heights use 20). A fraction below 1 has a minus log, so the loss is $-10\log_{10} T$.

cards.q: You want to know how much of the sound crosses from a wedge into a part. What do you need to know about each material?
options: Its density times its velocity: the impedance
cards.why: What crosses depends on the impedances, $Z = \rho v$, of both materials. Velocity alone is what you need for depth and timing ($d = \frac{vt}{2}$). Aluminium has a higher velocity than steel but well under half its impedance, so velocity alone would mislead.

cards.q: A steel plate: density 7850 kg/m³, velocity 5920 m/s. The back-wall echo is at {t} µs. How thick is the plate?
cards.why: Depth needs only the velocity and the time, halved for there and back: $d = \frac{vt}{2}$. The density only matters for impedance ($Z = \rho v$), which decides how **much** comes back, not **when**.
cards.hint: Which formula gives a distance from a time? Is the density needed for it?

cards.q: The first back-wall echo is at {a}% of screen height and the second at {b}%. How many dB lower is the second?
cards.why: Echo heights are **amplitudes**, so use $20\log_{10}$ of their ratio. Energies, like $R$ and $T$, use $10\log_{10}$. Same log, a different number in front: check which kind of ratio you have.
cards.hint: Is this a ratio of echo heights, or of energies?

cards.q: Oil ($Z_1$ = {z1} MRayl) couples a probe to aluminium ($Z_2$ = {z2} MRayl). What percentage of the intensity goes into the aluminium?
cards.why: Most of it comes back, as at any liquid to metal boundary, because the impedances are so far apart. What does not come back goes on: $T = 1 - R$.

cards.back: $Z = \rho v$ (density times velocity), in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, called rayl; usually quoted in MRayl.

cards.front: The share of intensity reflected at a boundary (normal incidence)?
